Historical name for the humane, nonrestraining asylum care of the late 18th and 19th centuries, linked to Tuke's York Retreat and to Pussin and Pinel in Paris.
A 19th-century pseudoscience that read character and mental faculties from the shape of the skull; useless as medicine but it placed mental illness in the brain.
Morel's 1852 term for a deteriorating illness starting in adolescence; Kraepelin's dementia praecox and Bleuler's schizophrenia grew from it.
Kraepelin's name for a psychosis of early onset with a long deteriorating course, later renamed schizophrenia by Bleuler.
Jean-Pierre Falret's 'circular insanity', alternating mania and melancholia; an early description of bipolar disorder.
Jules Baillarger's 1854 'double-form insanity', mania and depression in one illness; disputed priority with Falret's folie circulaire.
Popular name for Bethlem, the London hospital founded in 1247; the word came to mean uproar and confusion.
Adolf Meyer's approach, which saw each mental disorder as a person's reaction to life stress.
Also called the St. Louis criteria: the first systematic research criteria for 15 major psychiatric categories, from Washington University; a basis for the RDC and DSM-III.
The RDC of Spitzer, Endicott and colleagues, which expanded the Feighner criteria and led to DSM-III.
The first biologic theory of depression, supported by reserpine causing depression by depleting monoamines.
The move of psychiatric patients out of long-stay asylums into the community, spurred in the United States by the 1963 community mental health centers law.
